title: Natural-language analytics with Genie
summary: Place the Genie family's three roles, follow a North plant question from words to validated SQL, curate a Genie Agent so answers match the metric contract under each asker's permissions, and write a benchmark with a review loop that makes no live-agent claim.
objectives: Distinguish Genie One, Genie Agents and Genie Code by role and read each documentation page's own name for them.
Trace a question through interpretation, generated SQL, result and validation, and curate the inputs that keep it on contract.
Write a benchmark with expected SQL and result properties, authorized and unauthorized cases and misleading prompts, and a review process that makes no claim about a live space.

questions.prompt: test-outsider can open the North space but holds no SELECT on the accepted table, and asks 'What was line 3's rate on Thursday?'. The benchmark row marks the asker as not authorized. Which reply passes the row?

options.text: No rates, and a sentence saying the data is unavailable to this user.
options.rationale: Data access is evaluated as test-outsider, who holds no SELECT on the accepted table; the row expects no rows and an honest reason.

options.text: 4.8%, because the curator who saved the warehouse can read the table.
options.rationale: The curator's embedded credentials grant warehouse access only; they never extend data access to the asker.

options.text: An error that the warehouse is unavailable, because analysts lack CAN USE on it.
options.rationale: End users do not need direct warehouse permissions; the embedded credential supplies warehouse access, so this is not the expected failure.

options.text: The rate rounded to a whole percent, as a compromise.
options.rationale: A rounded rate is still data the identity may not read; an unauthorized case passes only with no rows.

questions.prompt: Which reply to 'How many defects did we have last week?' passes the ambiguous row in the North plant benchmark?

options.text: 'Do you mean defective units or rejected inspections? Only defective units are in this space.'
options.rationale: The row expects the readings named before any query, because the space holds one reading and not the other.
401 matches one reading, but answering without asking is a lucky guess that the ambiguous class exists to catch.

options.text: A count of rejected inspections from the raw inspections table.
options.rationale: Raw inspections are not in the space and are not contracted; reading them would be a wrong-table failure as well as a guess.
One reading is answerable from the accepted table, so a blanket refusal fails the asker and the row.

questions.prompt: A teammate's bookmark reads 'Use benchmarks in a Genie Space'. What should you conclude about the name?

options.text: It is the older name some pages still use for what the Genie Agents page now calls a Genie Agent.
options.rationale: The Genie Agents page says agents were formerly Genie Spaces, and several pages under the older path keep the older title.

options.text: Genie Spaces are a separate product that the benchmark feature belongs to.
options.rationale: Two names on two pages do not make two products; the pages describe the same curated environment.

options.text: The page is obsolete and its guidance should be ignored.
options.rationale: Pages under the older path are current documentation; only the name in the title lags the rename.

options.text: Genie Space is the name of Genie One's chat interface.
options.rationale: Genie One's chat searches dashboards, queries and agents; it is not called a Genie Space.

cards.prompt: A supervisor asks Genie One about line 3. Which Genie family member produces the SQL behind the answer?
cards.answer: A Genie Agent that the analyst curated for the North plant produces the SQL; Genie One is the entry point that routed the question.
cards.explanation: Genie One is the business-user interface whose chat searches dashboards, queries and Genie Agents. The agent is the configured environment with the tables, definitions, examples and instructions, so it turns the question into SQL and owns whether the answer follows the contract.

cards.prompt: A colleague's link is titled 'Use benchmarks in a Genie Space'. Is that a different product from a Genie Agent?
cards.answer: No. The Genie Agents page says agents were formerly Genie Spaces; some pages under the older path still use the older name.
cards.explanation: The rename is not uniform across the documentation, so each page is read in its own words. Treat Genie Space and AI/BI Genie space as search aliases for the same concept, and read the current page for behaviour rather than assuming the older page is obsolete.

cards.prompt: Genie names the right line but a rate 0.5 points too high. Where do you look first?
cards.answer: Read the generated SQL: an average of daily rates instead of a ratio of sums points to interpretation and missing business semantics.
cards.explanation: A right name with a wrong number usually means the table and filter were right and the arithmetic was not. The generated SQL shows the arithmetic directly; comparing it with the reference query over the same snapshot classifies the failure as wrong arithmetic, which the metric view fixes.

cards.prompt: What reply passes the ambiguous benchmark row for 'How many defects did we have last week?'
cards.answer: A clarifying question naming defective units and rejected inspections, then the chosen answer or a refusal with its reason.
cards.explanation: The space holds defective units (401 in the synthetic week) but not rejected inspections, which need raw data. A silent 401 happens to match one reading, yet it teaches the asker that the space guesses; the row therefore expects the question back before any number.

cards.prompt: Why keep raw inspections out of the North space although they hold more detail?
cards.answer: Every table in scope competes during interpretation, and the raw table's plain 'defects' column would win questions the contract answers.
cards.explanation: The curation guidance asks for five or fewer focused tables. Raw inspections include voided and duplicate versions and have no contract, so a question landing there is plausible, fast and wrong. Leaving a table out is a curation decision, not an access control; permissions still apply separately.

cards.prompt: What changes when a column called dr gains a description saying what it counts?
cards.answer: Interpretation can map words such as 'rate' to it with the right unit and arithmetic instead of guessing from a short name.
cards.explanation: Genie uses Unity Catalog names and descriptions to generate SQL. A description that says 'defective units over inspected units, never averaged across days' carries the contract into the step that chooses columns; the benchmark then checks whether the mapping improved.

cards.prompt: Predict line 2's five-day rate if SQL averages its daily rates of 6.2, 4.9, 7.0, 6.0 and 9.0 percent.
cards.answer: It reports 6.6%, while the contract's ratio of sums, 146 defective over 2,400 inspected units, gives 6.1%.
cards.explanation: Averaging rates weights day 5's 200 inspected units like day 2's 800, so the low-volume, high-rate day pulls the figure up. A metric view defining the measure once as SUM over SUM removes that choice from interpretation.

cards.prompt: In what order does the curation guidance rank datasets, SQL expressions, example SQL and text instructions?
cards.answer: Documented datasets first, then SQL expressions for business semantics, then example SQL, and text instructions only as a last resort.
cards.explanation: SQL definitions and examples are executed and can be checked; prose is reinterpreted on every question. Instructions that remain should name a trigger and an exact reply, and agree with the examples on details such as rounding.

cards.prompt: What does a Trusted label on a Genie response tell you, and what does it not?
cards.answer: It says a trusted asset, such as a parameterized example or SQL function, built the answer; it does not prove the question was understood.
cards.explanation: A misread question matched to the wrong trusted asset still carries the label, and a correct unlabelled answer is possible. Trusted assets need their own benchmark rows, including a phrasing that should not match them, and askers need EXECUTE on trusted functions.

cards.prompt: An author saved a warehouse on the space. Can a supervisor now read everything the author can read?
cards.answer: No. The embedded credential grants warehouse access only; each query's data access is evaluated with the supervisor's own permissions.
cards.explanation: The set-up page separates compute from data access. The author's credentials let every user run queries on the warehouse, while Unity Catalog checks each table, row filter and column mask as the end user. Unlike a dashboard published with shared data permissions, where every viewer's query runs with the publisher's data grants, a Genie Agent's saved credential covers compute only. That is why a curator's own test run says nothing about supervisors.

cards.prompt: Why does a benchmark row state expected SQL properties as well as an expected number?
cards.answer: Because a wrong query can produce a right-looking number, and some rows must pass without any number at all.
cards.explanation: Naming the table, filter and arithmetic catches a lucky wrong query; the ambiguous, cannot-answer, unauthorized and override classes pass only on a clarification, a refusal with reason, no rows or a kept definition. A number-only row cannot express any of those.

cards.prompt: An unauthorized benchmark case returns line 3's rate to test-outsider in an otherwise perfect run. What happens next?
cards.answer: The run is failed as a disclosure, curation changes pause, and the case goes to the access review rather than to instructions.
cards.explanation: A disclosure is not a curation problem: instructions cannot remove a privilege the identity holds. The access review checks group membership, grants, row filters and whether the run used the intended test identity; the benchmark is rerun and dated after the fix.

cards.prompt: Which kind of question should the North space refuse with a reason instead of answering?
cards.answer: Questions whose answers are not in its tables or definitions, such as causes, the East plant, next week or rework.
cards.explanation: A confident answer to an out-of-scope question can only come from a guess, and even a correct guess teaches the asker that the space knows things it does not. The expected reply names what is missing and where the question belongs.
